\chapter{Exchanging Names}
\label{ch:la-exchanging-names}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone's name in Latin and give my own, using the classical dative of possession.}

Ask quid tibi nōmen est? and answer mihi nōmen est, holding the possessor in the dative while the name itself may go either way.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...]{quid tibi nōmen est?, mihi nōmen est... — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}, the dative way}

\label{lesson:LA-C20-quid-tibi-nomen}



\begin{quote}
English says you \textbf{have} a name. German says you're \textbf{called} something. Latin does neither — it says the name \textbf{belongs to you}, using nothing but a case ending.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: quid tibi nōmen est? — literally \textquotedblleft{}what is the name TO YOU?\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Quid tibi nōmen est?} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what's your name?}\textquotedblright{}) is, word for word, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what} {[}is{]} \textbf{the-name} {[}to{]} \textbf{you}?\textquotedblright{} — no verb for \textquotedblleft{}have,\textquotedblright{} no verb for \textquotedblleft{}be called.\textquotedblright{} The name simply \textbf{exists}, and \textbf{tibi} (\textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} dative case) says who it belongs to.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mihi nōmen est... — the same construction, in reply}
The reply follows the identical pattern: \textbf{mihi nōmen est} {[}name{]} — \textquotedblleft{}{[}the-name{]} {[}is{]} to-me {[}name{]}.\textquotedblright{} This is Latin's genuine \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}dative of possession\textquotedblright{}}: instead of a possessive verb, the possessor simply sits in the dative case, and the thing possessed — here, \textbf{nōmen}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} — stays in the nominative, as the sentence's real subject.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quid tibi nōmen est?\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}what's the name to you?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mihi nōmen est...\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}the name is to me...\textquotedblright{}
  \item the case doing the work — dative \emph{tibi}/\emph{mihi}, not a verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What case does the possessor sit in, in \textbf{mihi nōmen est}? (\textbf{Dative} — \emph{mihi}, \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{}) Does Latin use a verb like \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}be called\textquotedblright{} for this? (\textbf{No} — the name simply exists; possession is shown by the dative case alone.) What noun remains the sentence's grammatical subject? (\textbf{Nōmen}, \textquotedblleft{}name.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puerō nōmen est Mārcus / Mārcō]{Mārcus or Mārcō? — a real classical variation}

\label{lesson:LA-C20-name-case-variation}



\begin{quote}
The possessor in Latin's naming construction is reliably dative. The personal name beside \textbf{nōmen}, however, is not locked to one case in every author.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: The stable frame}]
The dative possessor appears across authors from Plautus through Livy and Sallust:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{puerō nōmen est ...} — to the boy the name is ...
\end{quote}

That \textbf{puerō} does not change. It marks the person who possesses the name.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Two habits for the personal name}]
\textbf{Cicero} tends to keep the personal name nominative, agreeing with \textbf{nōmen}, the sentence's subject:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{puerō nōmen est Mārcus}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Livy} and \textbf{Sallust} more often pull the personal name into the dative to match the possessor:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{puerō nōmen est Mārcō}
\end{quote}

The underlying dative-of-possession construction is the same. The choice between \textbf{Mārcus} and \textbf{Mārcō} is authorial variation, not evidence that one sentence has stopped using the dative of possession.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}puerō\textquotedblright{} — to the boy; always the dative possessor
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mārcus\textquotedblright{} — Cicero's usual nominative pattern
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mārcō\textquotedblright{} — the matching dative found more often in Livy/Sallust
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Which case remains constant for the possessor? (\textbf{Dative.})
  \item Which author tends toward nominative \textbf{Mārcus}? (\textbf{Cicero.})
  \item Which authors more often use matching dative \textbf{Mārcō}? (\textbf{Livy and Sallust.})
  \item Do the two forms represent different possession constructions? (\textbf{No.})
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
